title: Harsh Ahuja vs Sunita Garg on 18 September, 2024
full_text: Harsh Ahuja vs Sunita Garg on 18 September, 2024 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg IN THE COURT OF Ms. MANU GOEL KHARB: SPECIAL JUDGE (NDPS)-02: SOUTH-WEST DISTRICT DWARKA COURTS:NEW DELHI Criminal Appeal No. 1880/2024 CRN No. DLSW01-003764-2024 In the Matter of : Sh. Harsh Ahuja S/o Sh. Harish Ahuja R/o P-45, 2nd D Floor, Vijay Vihar, Uttam Nagar New Delhi-110059 ....Appellant Versus Smt. Sunita Garg W/o Sh. Rakesh Garg, R/o H. No. 540, KG-1, Vikaspuri New Delhi-110018 ....Respondent Date of Institution of the Appeal : 18.04.2024 Date of Arguments : 28.08.2024 Date of Judgment : 18.09.2024 JUDGMENT: 1. Vide this judgment, I shall dispose of the present appeal under Section 374 Cr.P.C. filed by the appellant against the order of conviction dated 31.01.2024 and order on sentence dated 16.03.2024 passed by Ms. Vinerjeet Kaur, Ld. MM (NI Act)-03, Dwarka Courts, New Delhi in case bearing CC No. 42309/2019 titled as "Sunita Garg vs. Harsh Ahuja" whereby appellant was Page 1 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg convicted and sentenced to simple imprisonment till rising of the Court and has been directed to pay Rs. 61,600/- (Rupees Sixty One Thousand Six Hundred) to the respondent herein, which includes the principal loan amount and the interest computed thereupon @ 6% per annum for a period of two years and in default of payment of compensation, to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one month. 2. Appellant herein was the accused before the Ld. Trial Court and the respondent was the complainant before the Ld. Trial Court. For the sake of convenience, both the parties shall be addressed by the same nomenclature by which they were addressed before the Ld. Trial Court. 3. Brief facts of the case are that the accused/appellant was a tenant in the property of respondent i.e. C-14, First Floor, Milap Nagar, New Delhi-110059 on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 16,000/- (later on the same was reduced to Rs. 15,000/- on expiry of around two-three months of tenancy period) for residential purposes only, but accused was not regular in payment of the rent and committed default on various occasions and consequently, the accused was asked to vacate the tenanted premises on expiry of the tenancy period. The accused vacated the tenanted premises in the first week of September 2019 and there were outstanding dues of Page 2 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg Rs. 55,000/- towards the accused in respect of rent and pending electricity bill. In discharge of his legal liability to pay the outstanding dues, the accused issued a cheque for a sum of Rs. 55,000/- dated 18.10.2019 drawn on IndusInd Bank, Paschim Vihar, Delhi in favour of the complainant but the said cheque was returned unpaid vide return memo dated 21.10.2019 with the reason 'Stop Payment.' Complainant also sent legal notice dated 30.10.2019 via speed post to the accused intimating him about the dishonour of the cheque in question and calling upon the accused to make the payment of cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal notice but despite receipt of the said legal notice, accused failed to pay the cheque amount to the complainant. Thereafter, the complainant filed the complaint case under Section 138 of NI Act. 4. Complainant led pre-summoning evidence and the accused was summoned by the Ld. Trial court. After the appearance of accused, notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. was served to him to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial and took the defence that he had taken the flat of the complainant on rent and had given her security cheques against the said transaction. He further stated that he does not owe any liability to the complainant and that he had deposited the rent in the bank account of complainant and to prove the same he can furnish his bank statement. He stated that he had Page 3 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg issued a blank signed cheque and the rest of the particulars were not filled by him. He further stated that he receive the legal notice sent by the complainant and even replied to the same. 5. Complainant examined herself as CW1 in her post- summoning evidence. She tendered her post summoning evidence by way of affidavit Ex. CW1/A and relied upon the documents Ex. CW1/1 to Ex. CW1/4. Complainant further deposed that she was maintaining her bank account in Central Bank of India, Vikaspuri Branch, New Delhi and the cheque in question was presented for collection through that account. CW1 further deposed that the statutory demand notice was sent to the accused at his correct address. 6. The accused did not cross-examine the complainant despite several opportunities and his right to cross- examine the complainant's witness was closed by the Ld. Trial Court vide order dated 01.12.2022 and the matter was listed for statement of accused u/s 281 read with Section 313 Cr.P.C. In his statement u/s 281 read with Section 313 Cr.P.C., all the incriminating evidence was put to the accused and the accused stated that he made the entire payment of rent to the complainant and the complainant had misused the cheques by filing the present complaint 4 to 5 months after he had vacated Page 4 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg the rented accommodation. He further stated that he did not receive the notice but the address mentioned thereon is correct. He further averred that he did not owe any liability towards the complainant and the complainant has misused the cheque in question. 7. Thereafter, the accused led defence evidence and examined himself as DW-1. He deposed that he never took any loan from the complainant Sunita Garg. He further stated that he had taken a rented accommodation flat from the complainant to run PG for boys and the said payment of the rent has already been made to the complainant in the account of her husband Sh. Rakesh Garg through the account of the boys who were living as paying guest in the said flat. He further stated that the cheque in question was given as a security cheque to the complainant and the complainant had filed the present complaint 4-5 month after he had vacated the rented accommodation. DW1 was duly cross examined by the ld. Counsel for complainant and denied all the suggestions put to him by the ld. Counsel for complainant. Thereafter Defence Evidence was closed. 8. After hearing arguments, Ld. Trial Court vide its impugned judgment dated 31.01.2024 convicted the accused and sentenced him to simple imprisonment till rising of the Court and directed him to pay Rs. 61,600/- (Rupees Sixty One Thousand Six Hundred) to the Page 5 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg complainant which includes the principal loan amount and the interest computed thereupon @ 6% per annum for a period of two years and in default of payment of compensation, to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one month. 9. Feeling aggrieved, the accused has challenged the impugned order and sentence by filing the present appeal on the grounds mentioned below : (i) Ld. Trial court failed to appreciate the fact that the cheque in question was not issued by the appellant in discharge of liability and the complainant misused the cheque in question and further abused the process of law. (ii) That the appellant had given the cheques in question as security cheque. (iii) That the Ld. Trial Court has failed to take into consideration the fact that no legal demand notice was ever served upon the appellant as is mandatory under the provisions of NI Act . (iv) That the order of Ld. Trial Court seems to be perverse and contrary to the material on record and is full of infirmity in the reasoning assigned by Ld. Trial Court for convicting the accused/appellant. Further, presumption u/s 139 of the Act comes into existence only after the complainant discharges her initial burden to prove the existence of legally enforceable debt. Page 6 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg 10. Ld. counsel for the respondent argued that there is no infirmity in the order of the Ld. Trial Court and the Ld. MM has rightly convicted the accused after considering the material on record and prayed that appeal be dismissed. 11. I have heard detailed arguments heard on behalf of both the parties and have gone through the case file and carefully perusal the trial court record. 12. It is trite in law that in a prosecution under Section 138 NI Act, the statutory presumption under Section 118 & 139 NI Act stands in favour of the complainant and once the complainant proves that negotiable instrument/cheque is executed by the maker in favour of the holder of the cheque, the law presumes that the same is drawn for consideration and the holder of the cheque received it in discharge of any debt or legal liability. Thereafter, the burden shifts on the accused to prove the contrary, which he can do so by demolishing the credit of the complainant through his cross examination or by leading any cogent evidence in his defence and the burden on the accused is only of preponderance of probabilities and not as heavy as that on the prosecution. 13. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in " K. Bhaskaran Vs. SankaranVaidhya Balan (1999) 7 SCC 510 Page 7 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg summarized the ingredients of the offence U/s 138 NI Act . The relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference :- "The offence U/s 138 of the Act can be completed only with the concatenation of a number of acts. The following are the acts which are components of the said offence: (1) drawing of the cheque, (2) presentation of the cheque to the banker, (3) returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank, (4) giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque demanding the payment of the cheque amount, (5) failure of the drawer to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of notice." 14. As per record, the cheque in question was signed by the accused and the same was presented by the complainant to her banker but the cheque was returned unpaid by the bank with remarks 'Stop Payment'. Hence, the dishonor of the cheque in question in this case is not under dispute. 15. The first plea taken by the accused is that he never received the legal demand notice. Here, it would be relevant to notice that at the stage of notice under section 251 CrPC, accused stated that he had received the legal demand notice and that he also gave a reply to the notice whereas at the time of his statement under Section 313 CrPC, he took a contradictory stand and stated that he never received the legal demand notice. Page 8 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg 16. Under the provisions of Section 138 of NI Act, not only the giving of notice but also the receipt of notice has to be proved by the complainant. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has judicially recognized 'deemed or constructive service of notice' in various decisions. In the case of K. Bhaskar Vs. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan AIR 1999 SC 3762, it was held that : "If a strict interpretation is given that the drawer should have actually received the notice for the period of 15 days to start running, no matter that the payee sent the notice on the correct address, a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by different strategies and he could escape from the legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act. It must be borne in mind that the court should not adopt an interpretation which helps a dishonest evader and clips an honest payee as that would defeat the very legislative measure." 17. It was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that even in cases where the notice is returned as unclaimed, such date would be the commencing date in reckoning the period of 15 days as envisaged under proviso (c) of Section 138 NI Act provided notice was issued on the correct address of the accused. 18. The service of court summons by this court as well as by the Ld. Trial Court was effected upon the accused at the address of the accused mentioned in the legal notice which is the same address which was mentioned by him in the bail bond furnished before the Ld. Trial Court as well as the memo of parties filed before this court in the Page 9 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg appeal. As such, such the legal notice is deemed to be served upon the accused. 19. In view of the above discussion, it stands duly proved that legal demand notice was duly served upon the accused but the accused had failed to make the payment against the dishonored cheques within the stipulated period despite the service of legal demand notice and therefore, all the ingredients of the offence under Section 138 NI Act are proved. 20. Once the complainant was able to fulfill all the ingredients of the offence, the onus shifted upon the accused to prove his defence. So, in the present case, complainant has discharged her burden of a prima facie case by leading evidence and by satisfying the basic ingredients of Section 138 NI Act and now the burden shifted upon the accused to rebut the presumptions under Section 118 and 139 of NI Act operating in favour of the complainant. 21. Ld. counsel for the appellant argued that the accused had taken the flat of the complainant on rent and had given the cheque in question as security cheque against the said transaction. The accused also claimed that he had made the payment of the rent to the complainant and the present cheque was issued by way of security and not in discharge of any legal liability towards the Page 10 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg complainant. Ld. Counsel further argued that the accused was regularly depositing the rent in the bank account of complainant as shown in bank account statement of the accused Ex. DW1/A. 22. Coming to the facts of the present case, accused has relied upon the bank statement Ex. DW1/A to show that he had already made the payment into the account of the complainant but a bare perusal of the statement of account shows that there is a single entry dated 24.07.2019 of Rs. 6,000/- into the account of complainant. Apart from this there is no entry in the entire statement of account showing that the accused was regularly paying the rent to the complainant, which in turn, is corroborative of and fortifies the submissions made by the complainant that the accused was not regular in payment of rent. 23. It is also not out of place to mention that at the time of notice u/s 251 Cr.P.C., accused stated that he has deposited the rent in the bank account of the complainant and he can furnish his bank statement to prove the same whereas, in his defence evidence, he took a contrary stand and deposed that the payment of rent has already been made into the account of husband of the complainant through the account of the boys who were living as paying guests in the said flat. Firstly, this is the first time that the accused mentioned that he Page 11 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg was using the flat of the complainant for paying guest purposes and accused had not given the said version at the time of notice or statement u/s 313 Cr.P.C. Secondly, the accused can be clearly seen making contradictory statements because at one place he stated that he had deposited rent in bank account of complainant and on the other hand he submits that the rent was deposited by the paying guests into the bank account of the complainant's husband. Moreover, the accused has not been able to substantiate/corroborate his version with the help of any documentary evidence showing payments into the account of complainant or her husband. 24. It is an admitted fact that the accused had taken a flat on rent from the complainant. The accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question, hence, the issuance of cheque in question is not in dispute but the accused raised a plea that the cheque issued by the accused/appellant to the complainant/respondent was misused by the complainant/respondent. 25. A security cheque is a post dated cheque issued to a payee as a security for availing the option to present the same in case where the drawer fails to fulfill the future obligations arising from a transaction or a business deal. A security cheque acts as a surety for the person accepting such cheque and it is now a settled law that Page 12 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg dishonor of a post dated cheque i.e. a security cheque attracts culpability u/s 138 NI Act. The only test for application of Section 138 is whether there was a legally enforceable debt on the date mentioned in the cheque. In the case of 'Sripati Singh Vs. State of Jharkhand', Crl. A. No. 1269, 1270 of 2021, the division bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India opined that where a cheque is issued as security for a time specific loan, on default of repayment of loan the security cheque issued would mature, if then the security cheque is dishonored the consequences contemplated Section 138 of NI Act and other provisions of NI Act would flow. 26. Hence, the defence raised by the accused miserably fails and the appeal is liable to be dismissed on account of failure of the accused to prove that he has no legal liability towards the complainant for the cheque in question. 27. In the present case, the accused has not been able to establish his defence either through his own evidence or by way of impeaching the credit of complainant's witnesses and it appears that he raised a false defence in order to avoid his legal liability towards the complainant for the cheque in question. Consequently, there is hardly any ground to interfere with the judgment of conviction given by the Ld. Trial Court. Page 13 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg Thereafter, grounds of appeal taken by the accused is rejected. 28. Ld. Trial Court has passed a well-reasoned and detailed judgment discussing all the contentions raised by both the parties. In view of the above, the court does not find any reason to interfere in the impugned judgment dated 31.01.2024 passed by the Ld. Trial Court. The judgment of Ld. Trial Court is well-reasoned and the trial court has given a legally sound decision and deserves to be upheld. 29. So far as the sentence is concerned, Ld. Trial Court has sentenced the appellant/accused to imprisonment till the rising of the court and pay a sum of Rs. 61,600/- as fine to the complainant/respondent within 30 days and in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one month. This court is of the view that the Ld. Trial Court had already shown sufficient leniency by sentencing the accused only to imprisonment till the rising of the court and fine of Rs. 61,600/- only and hence no further leniency is required to be shown to the accused. 30. For the aforesaid reasons, the appeal filed by the accused Harsh Ahuja is hereby dismissed and the judgment and order on sentence dated 31.01.2024 and 16.03.2024 passed by the Ld. Trial Court is accordingly upheld. Page 14 of 15 CA No. 1880/2024 Harsh Ahuja Vs. Sumita Garg 31. Trial court record be sent back to the Ld. Trial Court/Successor court alongwith a copy of this judgment. Ld. Trial court is directed to execute the sentence as per law. 32. Appeal file be consigned to record room after due compliance. Pronounced in the open Court today MANU by Digitally signed MANU GOEL KHARB i.e. 18.09.2024 GOEL Date: 2024.09.18 KHARB 17:12:11 +0000 (Manu Goel Kharb) Special Judge, (NDPS) -02, Dwarka Courts, New Delhi Page 15 of 15
